explanation: Mixture. Fires on ' College'/' University' after an institution's proper name (Hollins College, Churchill College, Wesleyan University). It also fires on inner subword pieces of rare or technical words (judicata, anhydrase, PREPROCESSOR, Clackmannanshire, Cyberpunk, PUBG) and on the GPL boilerplate '(at your option)'. Ordinary prose gives weak or no activation.

Fires on a token in the middle of a fixed multiword proper name or title. Strongest is ' the' in US court names ('Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit', 'District Court for the Western District of ...'). It is also strong on the inner word of named phrases such as 'Seven Against Thebes', 'Big Five', 'New World', 'Old Spanish Trail' and 'Global Compact'. Generic 'for the' outside a name is weak.

Fires on police and arrest words in crime-news reporting: 'Arrested', 'arrested', 'caught', 'taken into custody', 'pulled over', 'drove away from'. It needs the law-enforcement context. There are some unrelated weaker hits (College of, hive, LaTeX '{', personality disorder).

No clear theme. Fires on function words or short continuation tokens in the middle of a clause, often after a comparative or evaluative phrase ('superior in', 'slowed as', 'pilot alike', 'Which is bigger', 'all copies'). It also fires on symbols in generated math word problems. The examples share no common topic.

Mostly fires on a non-initial subword piece that completes a word split across tokens: ant|iques, Ant|iepileptic, ent|ice, Sevent|y, Fort|y, inad|vis|able, filebrows|erview. It also fires on ' Town' in 'Cape Town'. Mid-range activations fall on sentence-final punctuation and are less specific.

Fires in narrative fiction or story-like prose. Typical spots are the token that starts a new sentence or paragraph ('The', '“You'), a past-tense action verb after a character's name ('Verosus sent', 'Austin stood', 'she reached', 'took'), and quote-closing punctuation after dialogue ('Portman said'). Expository or technical text gives little activation.

Strongest on the auxiliary ' has'/' have' right after a subject noun phrase, especially in scientific abstracts ('FFA exposure has been shown', 'It has recently been reported', 'NETs have'). A second job is ' a' in sports-score phrasing ('take a 25-', 'in a Sunday night maul', 'held on for a two-point win'). Degree words ' most'/' very' also fire.

Fires on tokens in Spanish, Portuguese or Italian text: word pieces like quer|do, Alc|uni, quit|ando, and words like ' tal', ' igual'. It also fires on Hispanic or Latin-American names in English text, mainly ' Mexican' and ' Angeles' in 'Los Angeles', plus San Diego and San Gabriel. Other text gives little or no activation.

Mixture. Fires on inner subword pieces of drug and biochemical names (methot|rex|ate, lumefantr|ine, interleuk|in, ranibiz|um|ab, dehydrogen|ase) and on later words of multiword agency or program names ('Mental Health', 'Health Promotion', 'High Energy Physics'). It also fires on interjections (Shh, Phew) and on digits inside statute numbers or ports.

Fires mainly in programming and technical Q&A text: the word after a code prompt ('that, given', 'return', '(string', '.com' in URLs, 'while', 'Control'). A second, smaller job is quantifier or comparison phrases in technical prose: 'at least', 'less than', 'per ticket', 'not just'.

Fires on the determiner or the start of the object right after a verb or preposition in ordinary prose, especially ' a' in 'on a', 'for a', 'such a' and 'is a', and on verbs after 'to' ('prefer to use', 'attempt to access'). The marked token opens the complement noun phrase or verb phrase. Context matters more than the token's identity.

Mixture of technical tokens. Fires on code and query identifiers or keywords (SQL 'FAST', 'PARTITIONED', 'syntax', LLVM '@', Haskell '{', import paths, 'md' keys), on file-format acronyms (WMV), on 'WRIT' in legal 'writ of mandamus', and on technical or legal noun phrases ('schedule 1 substance', 'sexual minorities', 'digital-to-analog'). There is no single theme.

Fires on keywords or line-initial tokens in source code and config files: 'struct' after a Go type name, 'class', 'function', 'with lib;', 'address:' in YAML, SQL 'like'/'UPDATE', Ruby 'alias each', and a capitalized word that starts a prose line just after a code block. Natural-language prose without code is near zero.

Fires on the first subword piece of a rare proper name or uncommon word split into several tokens: ' V'(opak), ' Kos'(kinen), 'ESS' in MESSER, ' Mil'(pitas), ' Ind'(ividually), ' res'(veratrol/ins/urfaced), 'W'(ess|elsbron). The word must start a multi-token split. Common whole-word tokens are weak.

Fires in formal expository sentences that define or describe something. It hits the word right after a descriptive noun or adjective that continues the description: 'features with', 'simple, specific', 'his many contributions', 'one of the leading causes', 'relatively infrequent but', 'source familiar'. These are mostly prepositions, conjunctions and attributive adjectives. The pattern is diffuse.

No consistent pattern. Top hits mix a subword in a math name (Plancher|el), noun heads in academic prose ('genetic diversity', 'nutritional status', 'microcomputer system'), possessives and pronouns ('its', 'your', 'they') and code fragments (C#, PRIMARY KEY, __clone).

Fires on bracket or symbol clusters in code and regex ('(.', '([^', '[*]', '."\', '[{'') and on '+/-' in reported statistics ('120 +/- 34'). It also fires on the second piece of camelCase identifiers (arrayOf, getCurrent, numberOf) and on ' southeastern'. It is mostly symbol-heavy notation.

Mixture of formatting and boilerplate tokens: citation markers after '[@' ('b', 'B' in '[@b0055]'), the last dot of '. . .' ellipses, 'address:' in YAML front matter, header names after '#include <', '(c)' in license headers, and the Spanish '¿'. There is no single semantic theme.

Fires on punctuation that links a key to its value or an argument to its call in code and URLs: '=' in URL query strings (?id=, ?page=, user=), '['' in PHP array indexing ($_POST['), ':' in Objective-C method arguments (forKey:@", numberWithFloat:), '":"' in JSON, and '\frac' in LaTeX. Line breaks in prose are weak.

Fires on the token right after a short sentence-opening subject: copulas and contractions after demonstratives ('That's', 'that is', 'These are', '…” is'), and the comma after a speaker name before or after a quote ('Graham said,', 'Mr. Romano,'). A second job is the period or comma plus line break ending a line in legal case captions ('Fifth Circuit.\n', 'UNITED STATES OF AMERICA,').

Fires on function parameters and arguments in source code: parameter names and defaults in signatures ('b = None', 'innerRadius', 'propertyValue', '*args', 'repeat=None') and literal arguments in call lists (', 0, 0', '0x00', 'false', 'flex: 1'). A weaker side effect is inner digits of numbers in prose, such as years and coordinates.
